thread.title_full: Men Leave Workforce by Millions, Raising Alarm - NewsBreak

author: Jim Mishler
title: Men Leave Workforce by Millions, Raising Alarm - NewsBreak
text:
By Jim Mishler ,
9 hours ago
(Dreamstime)
Millions of men are leaving the workforce, and analysts say the trend threatens the nation's social stability, The Washington Times reported Wednesday.
The Times cited the latest Bureau of Labor Statistics breakdown showing 44.07 million of 132.8 million men 16 and older (33.2%) were not in the labor force last month.
That figure is 9 million more than in 2012, a 29% increase, according to the report.
The number of men not in the labor force rose by 891,000 over the preceding 12 months alone, the Times reported, attributing the shift in part to the loss of manufacturing and finance jobs.
But the population figures underlying that analysis rest on Census Bureau estimates that the bureau itself says have grown harder to pin down.
The Census Bureau reported in January that net international migration fell from 2.7 million people in 2024 to 1.3 million in 2025, and is projected to drop further to about 321,000 in 2026 if current trends continue.
The bureau said the 2025 figure covers July 2024 through June 2025, a period spanning two U.S. administrations and changes in immigration policy.
Complete data covering that period will not be released until December, the bureau said.
The Census Bureau also found that the foreign-born population measured in the Current Population Survey, the same survey the Bureau of Labor Statistics uses to calculate workforce participation, fell from 53.3 million in January 2025 to 51.9 million in June 2025.
The bureau cautioned that the decline "can also reflect survey non-response, coverage error or the impact of population controls," rather than an actual drop in population.
The bureau also revised its migration methodology in December 2024 after determining its prior estimates failed to capture recent shifts in the data, and it updated population figures dating back to 2020 as a result.
According to the report, the share of men 16 and older participating in the workforce dropped from 77.5% in 1976 to 66.8% last month, the lowest non-pandemic reading since 1948.
The share of women 16 and older in the workforce climbed from 47.3% in 1976 to 56.4% over the same period, according to the report.
"The American economy has gradually moved away from some of the industries that historically provided good jobs to men without college degrees," Scott Beaulier, a University of Wyoming economist, told the Times.
"Meanwhile, much of the recent employment growth has occurred in areas such as healthcare and education, where women make up a much larger share of the workforce," he said.
The American Staffing Association told the Times that increased retirements, recent immigration restrictions and a rise in boys struggling academically have driven the trend, though the group did not cite data isolating the effect of immigration policy.
The trade group estimates the number of men leaving the workforce after turning 65 has jumped by 99% since 2000, compared with a 71% increase among women, the Times reported.
"Decreased workforce participation among men poses serious issues for the economy," Noah Yosif, the staffing association's chief economist, said. "Bringing more men into the workforce is just as important as preserving the gains of women within it."
The Times also cited automation in male-dominated industrial jobs as a contributing factor.
Analysts quoted in the report said the decline in working men adds to skilled worker shortages, reduces gross domestic product, shrinks the Social Security tax base, and increases male suicide and depression rates.
Not every analyst cited agreed with that framing.
"We shouldn't assume every nonworking man is dysfunctional," Peter Earle, a senior economist at the American Institute for Economic Research, told the Times. "Some are students, caregivers, disabled or financially able to remain outside the workforce."
White House spokesman Kush Desai told the Times that last month's 89.2% workforce participation rate for men aged 25 to 54 "remains above its monthly average over the last 10 years," which included a dip during the pandemic.
"The Trump administration is focused on investing in workforce training and accelerating economic growth to get more working-age Americans off the sidelines and playing an active role in America's resurgence," Desai said in an emailed statement to the Times.
